title: Wool and shellfish
hook: Marcus strips glamour: a purple robe is sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood (Meditations 6.13)
tomorrow: don't be turned into a Caesar

segments.voice: Last week ended with donkey's gone: a traveler who sang about his own loss. Know what you sing.

The sneakers with the right logo. The car in the driveway you slow down to look at. The watch that costs more than a year of groceries. Some things glow, as if owning one would change who a person is. A new week starts today, and it's called seeing clearly. It opens with a man who wore the purple of Rome, and who sat down one night and described it in the plainest words he could find.
screen: `SOME THINGS GLOW.` → `A WEEK OF SEEING CLEARLY.` → `WOOL AND SHELLFISH.`

segments.voice: In Rome, the color of power was purple. Not crayon purple: a deep dye that came from shellfish and cost a fortune. The emperor wore it. Marcus wore that robe. And in Book Six he wrote this about it, in George Long's translation: "this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shell-fish." He does the same with dinner. A fancy dish of meat is the dead body of a fish, or a bird, or a pig. Fine Italian wine is a little grape juice. He isn't sneering at food or wine. He's practicing a way of seeing: strip away the glow and look at what a thing actually is. Why would an emperor bother? Because, Marcus says in the same passage, outward show is one of the great deceivers of the mind. The moment you're most sure a thing is important is the moment it's most likely fooling you. So he lays such things bare and strips off the words that puff them up. This isn't about despising nice things. Wool is lovely. Wine can be a gift. It's about taking back the power you've handed to them. When the car in the driveway turns back into metal, glass and a loan, you're free to like it, or not, without it owning a piece of you. Your line: metal, glass and a loan.
screen: `THE COLOR OF POWER WAS PURPLE.` · `SHEEP'S WOOL DYED WITH SHELLFISH BLOOD.` · `OUTWARD SHOW DECEIVES THE MIND.` · then, large: `WOOL AND SHELLFISH.`

segments.voice: Let one thing with a glow come to mind, something you own, or want, or envy, and describe it the way Marcus would: what is it made of, where did it come from, what is it underneath the name? Notice whether the glow changes; you don't have to stop liking it.
Outward show. Marcus called it one of the great deceivers of the mind, and stripped his own purple robe down to sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood to see past it. Today's word.
Your line: metal, glass and a loan. You are still free to like it, glow or no glow. Day one hundred ninety-nine, in plain words.

screen: `DAY 199 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DON'T BE TURNED INTO A CAESAR.`

howItsDone: Many readers of the Stoics practice this plain description, sometimes called seeing things as they are, and use it on status objects, praise and cravings alike.

what it means: see what a thing actually is, and its glow loses its grip on you.
what a scholar hears: the Stoic practice of the physical definition, describing a thing in bare terms, and porphyra, the purple dye taken from shellfish.
